headline: Tech Selloff Sparks a Bond Rally, Pulling Rates Lower
tileReason: The daily 30-year average fell to 7.30% Thursday, its lowest in a month, as investors fled tech stocks for the safety of bonds.
takeaway: Mortgage rates took their biggest one-day step down in weeks on Thursday. The daily 30-year average fell 0.10% to 7.30%, the lowest since late September. The reason was a sharp selloff in tech stocks: worries about how much big companies are spending on artificial intelligence sent the Nasdaq down about 2.6%, and investors moved that money into the safety of Treasury bonds and mortgage bonds. That demand pushed the 10-year Treasury yield down roughly 0.17% to about 4.96%, its first close below 5% in a month. Freddie Mac's weekly survey also fell, to 7.32% from 7.40%, its first decline since August. This morning bonds are giving back a little of that rally: the 10-year yield is up about 0.03% to near 4.99%. Oil is the main reason. Brent crude jumped to around $116 a barrel, its highest since mid-2022, on new attacks on Saudi targets and talk of renewed U.S. strikes on Iran. Business surveys out this morning also showed strong growth and the fastest rise in selling prices in more than four years, which keeps inflation worries alive. Lenders may price a touch higher today than yesterday. Over the next month the odds look roughly balanced, with a slight lean toward rates staying about where they are.

Thursday's close was about 4.95%–4.96% depending on the source (Treasury's par curve 4.96%; market quotes 4.953%–4.957%), down from 5.13% Wednesday, the biggest one-day drop in more than a year.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Oct 28
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via Yahoo Finance (Oct 22, late day) and Trading Economics (Oct 23)
fedOdds.note: CME FedWatch put the odds of a hike on October 28 at about 7% late Thursday, down from about 28% a week earlier (Yahoo Finance); Trading Economics shows roughly a 91% chance of no change this morning, about 9% for a hike. Prediction market Polymarket was lower still, near 6%. December hike odds slipped but remain high: about 78% (FedWatch via Yahoo, late Thursday, from about 86% at midday) versus about 76% to 80% (Trading Economics, Oct 23). Reports of the October 14 post-CPI peak range from 44% to 54%. The Fed is in its quiet period before the meeting, so no official comments are expected.

drivers.title: Tech selloff sends money into bonds
drivers.text: Tech stocks fell hard on Thursday, with the Nasdaq down about 2.6% and chip stocks down nearly 7%, as disappointing results and huge AI spending plans at big companies like Meta made investors nervous. Much of that money moved into Treasury bonds and mortgage bonds, which are seen as safer. More buyers push bond prices up and yields down: the 10-year Treasury yield fell about 0.17% in one day, and mortgage rates followed it lower.

drivers.title: Oil climbs to its highest level since 2022
drivers.text: Brent crude rose to around $116 a barrel this morning, up roughly 2.5% and its highest since June 2022. Iran-aligned Houthi forces attacked Saudi targets including the Red Sea port of Yanbu, Saudi Aramco reportedly told staff to leave its Dhahran headquarters, and reports say the U.S. and Israel have planned more strikes on Iran after the midterm elections. Expensive energy feeds inflation, and bond investors demand higher yields when they expect inflation to stay high. That is a big part of why yields are edging back up this morning.

drivers.title: Business surveys show strong growth and rising prices
drivers.text: S&P Global's early October surveys of purchasing managers (PMIs, a quick read on business activity) showed the economy still growing fast, and companies raised their selling prices at the quickest pace in more than four years, partly because of oil. Strong growth plus rising prices gives the Fed reason to keep rates high or raise them, which tends to keep a floor under mortgage rates.

drivers.title: Odds of a Fed hike next week fade
drivers.text: Futures markets now see only about a 7% to 9% chance the Fed raises rates on October 28, down from more than 25% a week ago. A December hike is still seen as likely (roughly 76% to 80%), but those odds slipped a bit Thursday. Fewer expected hikes take a little pressure off yields.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates are still unusually far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The daily 30-year average is running about 2.3% above the 10-year Treasury yield, compared with a more typical 2.0%. That extra cushion means mortgage rates have room to improve if markets calm down, even without a further drop in Treasury yields.

outlook.basis: It's close to a coin flip, with a slight lean toward steady and a small tilt toward a bounce after Thursday's big drop. Working in borrowers' favor: nervous stock markets keep money flowing into bonds, Fed hike odds for next week have faded, and mortgage rates are still unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.3% vs. a typical 2.0%). Working against them: oil near $116 is the highest since 2022, business surveys show prices rising at the fastest pace in four years, and a December Fed hike is still widely expected. Big swing events: the October 28 Fed decision, the October 29 inflation (PCE) data, the November 6 jobs report, the November 10 CPI report, and any escalation in the Gulf.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average dropped to about 7.30% Thursday, the lowest in a month and down from roughly 7.5% in early October. Bonds are giving back a little of that this morning, and the Fed meets October 28 with key inflation data the next day, so it's worth asking your lender how locking now, a float-down option, or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Even with rates easing, buyers are stretched and choosy, and applications keep falling. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to buy down their rate, can help your home stand out while rates are lower than they were a few weeks ago.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: A tech-stock selloff pushed money into bonds and pulled mortgage rates down to about 7.30%, a one-month low, though surging oil prices are keeping a lid on further drops.
